content: What business outcomes and day-to-day operational decisions do you need this system to support around water-use regulation and resource management?

We need it to help staff quickly see whether permitted users are staying within their allowed allocations and where actual use is trending above or below what we expected. On the day-to-day side, it should support decisions like identifying compliance concerns, prioritizing inspections or follow-up, and understanding seasonal or regional demand patterns. Longer term, we want it to help evaluate whether management rules are actually reducing stress on the resource and to give us better evidence when adjusting permit conditions or planning for future demand.

Are there specific management-rule questions you need the system to answer when staff are assessing whether permitted users are within their allocations—such as how to treat overages, shortfalls, or other boundary cases in compliance and follow-up decisions?

Yes, those are exactly the kinds of questions we need it to help with. Staff need to know when a permittee is slightly over an allocation versus materially over, whether repeated shortfalls or overages over time should trigger a different review, and how to handle cases where use is seasonal or data is incomplete. We also need the system to flag boundary cases consistently so staff can apply the same rule the same way instead of relying on manual judgment each time.

As you think about how staff will actually use this in their day-to-day work, what constraints or conditions in your environment could affect how the system is delivered or used, such as where it needs to run, who needs access to it, or how it needs to fit with your existing processes?

It needs to work in our District environment and be accessible to internal staff, with some level of access for external customers as well. Since a lot of our work is GIS-based, it has to fit with the mapping and data tools we already use, and it needs to support existing review and reporting processes rather than forcing a completely new workflow. We also have to be careful about data permissions, because some regulatory and customer information can’t be broadly exposed.
When staff need to follow those existing review and reporting processes, what are the key steps, handoffs, or exceptions the system should support so they can keep working the way they do today?

Staff typically start by pulling the relevant permit and usage data, then comparing actual use against authorized limits over a chosen time period and area. If something looks off, it usually moves to a manual review or follow-up with the permittee, and then the findings get folded into a report or internal decision memo. The main exceptions are when data is missing, late, or clearly incomplete, because those cases need to be flagged rather than treated as a normal compliance result.
To make sure I understand the data and mapping side of this work, what internal District datasets do staff rely on most when they do this analysis, and how do those sources fit together in practice?

The main ones are the permit records, actual water-use reporting data, and the GIS layers for service areas, well locations, and other resource boundaries. In practice, staff use the permit data to understand what was authorized, the usage data to see what happened, and the spatial layers to tie both to a location and a management area. Sometimes we also need supporting layers like county or basin boundaries, but the core work really depends on those permit and usage sources lining up cleanly.
How often do the permit records, water-use reports, and GIS layers need to be refreshed, and what should the system do when one source updates before the others or a data load arrives late?

The timing can vary by source, so we don’t expect everything to update at exactly the same moment. In general, the system should be able to show the most recent load from each source and make it obvious when one dataset is newer than the others, because staff need to know whether they’re looking at a complete picture or a partial one. If a load is late, it should flag that status rather than quietly blending old and new data in a way that could mislead someone.
Thinking about the District employees who use these analyses, how do the different roles work together in practice, and what does each role need the system to help them do?

Different people use it at different points in the process. Analysts need to run the comparisons, map the results, and spot trends or anomalies, while managers and reviewers need a clearer summary so they can make compliance or resource-management decisions without digging through every record. Some staff may also need to prepare outputs for external communication or internal reporting, so the system should support both detailed investigation and higher-level review.

When staff review actual water-use reporting data, what rules should the system use to handle missing, estimated, corrected, or otherwise exceptional records so they can tell what really happened without misreading the report?

The system should clearly distinguish reported values from estimated or corrected ones, and it should keep the original record history visible so staff can see what changed and why. Missing records should be flagged as missing rather than treated as zero, and estimated data should be labeled so it doesn’t get mistaken for an actual reported value. If a correction comes in later, staff need to see both the current value and the prior version for audit and review purposes.

When a permit identifier is associated with more than one facility or parcel, or a facility or parcel has multiple permit identifiers, what business rule should the system follow to show that linkage clearly for staff?

It should show the relationship as many-to-many rather than forcing a single one-to-one match, because that’s often how the records exist in practice. Staff need to be able to see all linked facilities, parcels, and permit identifiers together, with the primary association clearly marked if there is one. If there’s any ambiguity or overlap, the system should flag it so someone can review it instead of hiding the complexity.
What actual water-use values does the system need to store and report, and at what time intervals should those measurements be organized, such as daily, monthly, or by reporting period?

We need to store the actual reported use values as they come in from the reporting process, and in some cases the system will also need derived totals or summaries for analysis. I’d expect most staff to work with monthly and annual or reporting-period views, since that’s how a lot of the regulatory work is done, but I’m not certain whether we need to retain daily values everywhere or only where they’re available. If daily data exists for some sources, the system should be able to accommodate it without forcing everything into the same interval.

Are there any business rules for how water-use measurements should be recorded or reported when different records use different units, including whether the system should convert them to a standard unit or preserve the original unit as reported?

Yes, the system should preserve the original unit as reported, because staff may need to trace back to the source exactly as it was submitted. At the same time, it should convert values to a standard unit for comparison and analysis so the maps and summaries are consistent across records. If a conversion is applied, the system should make that obvious and retain the original value and unit alongside the converted one.

What level of boundary precision do you need for the spatial objects used to locate and aggregate water-use information—for example, should the system support parcel-level, facility-level, or other specific boundary detail when records sit near or cross a border?

We need enough precision to support parcel-level and facility-level analysis, since staff often look at permit and use patterns tied to those boundaries. If a record falls near or crosses a boundary, the system should not just snap it silently to one side; it should preserve the geometry or at least flag the uncertainty so users know it may affect the aggregation. For some reporting, broader area boundaries may also be useful, but parcel and facility detail is the main need.
To shape the first release, what kinds of water-use analysis do staff most need to do with these records, and what business decisions or day-to-day tasks should that analysis support?

The first release should let staff compare permitted versus actual use, look at trends over time, and identify places where use is unusually high, low, or changing quickly. That supports day-to-day work like reviewing compliance, preparing internal summaries, and checking whether management rules appear to be affecting demand. It would also help them answer questions from supervisors or the public without having to build each analysis manually.

When staff use these analyses day to day, are there any specific conditions or exceptions that change how they should compare permitted versus actual use, identify unusual patterns, or interpret whether management rules are affecting demand?

Yes, there are a few practical exceptions. A permit might be active but not fully developed yet, or a facility may have seasonal operations, so actual use can look low without indicating a problem. Staff also need to account for reporting gaps, estimates, corrections, and special operating conditions like drought restrictions or temporary shutdowns, because those can change how a trend should be read.

When a permit is active but the site is still being developed, or when a facility is seasonal or temporarily shut down, how should the system decide whether low actual use should be treated as normal, flagged, or excluded from trend comparisons?

It probably should not decide that automatically in every case. I’d expect the system to let staff classify those situations with a status or exception flag, and then exclude or de-emphasize those records in trend comparisons when appropriate. If the status is unknown, the system should surface it as a potential outlier rather than assuming the low use is normal.

When staff need to compare trends across records that come in at different intervals, what rules should the system use to line up monthly, annual, reporting-period, and any daily data so the comparisons stay meaningful without forcing everything into one interval?

The system should support comparing at the native reporting interval first, and then let users roll records up to a common view when they need to compare them. For example, monthly data can be summarized to annual totals, but the system should avoid averaging away important spikes if the user is looking for anomalies. If intervals don’t align cleanly, it should make that mismatch visible and not silently combine records in a misleading way.

Are there any jurisdictional or reporting boundaries, such as district, state, basin, or permit-specific reporting limits, that change which water-use rules apply or how records should be interpreted and reported?

Yes, those boundaries matter a lot. District boundaries and basin boundaries can change which rules or review criteria apply, and permit-specific reporting limits can affect what staff expect to see in the data. The system should respect those boundaries in analysis and reporting, and it should make it clear which rule set or jurisdiction a record falls under.

When a record could fall under more than one jurisdiction or reporting limit, how should the system decide which one governs the analysis and what should staff see when there is a conflict or overlap?

In those cases, the system should follow a clear hierarchy of governing rules that the district can configure, because the right answer may depend on the specific program or permit. If there is a conflict or overlap, staff should see both the governing rule used and the competing boundary or limit so they can review it manually. It should never hide the conflict, since that would make the analysis hard to trust.

For file exchanges or GIS integrations, are there any file formats, coordinate systems, or geospatial standards the system must support or reject, and under what conditions would a different format be acceptable?

I know we’ll need standard GIS formats, but I don’t know the full approved list yet. At minimum, I’d expect common formats like shapefiles and geodatabase exports, plus whatever tabular files are used for water-use reporting, as long as the spatial reference is clearly defined. If a different format is proposed, it would need to be agreed to by the district GIS staff and proven to preserve the geometry, attributes, and coordinate system correctly.

When a file is in an otherwise supported GIS format but has missing or inconsistent geometry, attributes, or coordinate system information, what should the system do with it and how should staff be notified?

If the file is incomplete or inconsistent, the system should not load it silently. It should reject the bad records, log the specific issues, and show staff a clear import error message that says what failed and what needs to be fixed. If only part of the file is usable, I’d expect the system to accept the valid pieces but still flag the import as partial so someone can review it.

When moving from the manual or semi-automated process to the new system, what data cleanup or conversion, if any, should be done before import, and how should the system handle records that can’t be converted cleanly?

We should do as much cleanup as practical before import, especially for duplicate permits, inconsistent site names, and obvious coding differences, but I would not want the system to assume every legacy record is clean. If a record can’t be converted cleanly, it should be quarantined or flagged for manual review rather than forced in with guessed values. Staff need a way to see what was changed during conversion and what was left unresolved.
Looking ahead, what kinds of future changes or enhancements do you expect this system to need, and how should staff manage those changes without disrupting day-to-day work?

I’d expect future changes around new reporting rules, additional data sources, revised GIS layers, and maybe new comparison views or dashboards. Those changes should be handled through configuration or versioned updates where possible, so day-to-day users aren’t disrupted. Staff should be able to keep using the current ruleset while a new one is tested and approved, then switch over in a controlled way.

For permitted water-use records, what specific conditions or events should trigger a new version of a record or rule set, and how should staff distinguish and use the active version versus any superseded versions when reviewing permits or reports?

A new version should be triggered when a permit is modified, renewed, transferred, suspended, or otherwise materially changed, and also when a governing rule or reporting threshold changes. For analysis, staff should always see the active version as the default, but they also need access to prior versions for audit and historical comparison. Superseded versions should be clearly labeled with effective dates and status so nobody accidentally uses an old rule or permit condition in a current report.

When a new reporting rule, data source, GIS layer, or dashboard is introduced, what practical conditions should determine whether it is added as a configuration change versus a versioned release, and are there any cases where staff should continue using the existing view or rule set until the new one is proven in parallel?

If the change is just a label, a threshold, a layer refresh, or another adjustment that does not change the business logic, I’d treat that as configuration. If it changes how records are interpreted, calculated, or displayed in a meaningful way, it should be a versioned release so we can keep the old behavior available for audit and comparison. Yes, I do think staff should keep using the existing view or rule set in parallel when the new one is still being validated, especially if it affects official reporting or regulatory decisions.

Looking ahead, what specific kinds of changes to the District’s internal analysis and mapping datasets—such as updates, replacements, added fields, or new source datasets—should be treated as a new version versus a routine refresh, and what should happen if staff need to compare the old and new data side by side?

A routine refresh would be something like a monthly or quarterly update where the structure stays the same and we’re just getting newer records. A new version makes more sense when a dataset is replaced, the schema changes, fields are added or removed in a way that affects analysis, or the source itself changes enough that results could differ. If staff need to compare old and new side by side, the system should keep both versions available with clear effective dates and let them run the same analysis against each one without overwriting the earlier data.

When a new dataset version is approved, what should the controlled cutover look like in practice—who decides when to switch, what happens to any in-flight analysis or reports, and is there any fallback if the new version causes issues after go-live?

I’d expect the responsible program manager or data owner to approve the switch, with IT or GIS staff handling the actual release. In-flight analyses and reports should finish on the version they started with, and anything new should default to the approved version after the cutover. If problems show up after go-live, we should be able to roll back to the prior version quickly until the issue is fixed.

Are there any circumstances where you would delay, limit, or partially roll back a cutover—such as a high-impact reporting period, a downstream system dependency, or a validation issue—and who should make that call?

Yes, definitely. If we’re in a high-impact reporting period, or if a downstream system depends on the old structure, or if validation shows unexpected differences, I’d want to delay or do a partial rollback rather than force the cutover. That call should be made by the business owner for the dataset or report, with input from IT, GIS, and the operational staff who use it every day.

For missing, estimated, or corrected water-use records, what should the system do in day-to-day reporting and review when a record is later revised, a value is estimated after the fact, or no measurement is available for a period?

If a record is revised later, the system should keep the original value in the history and show the corrected value as the current one, with a clear audit trail of when and why it changed. If a value has to be estimated after the fact, it should be flagged as estimated so staff can distinguish it from measured data in reports and analysis. If no measurement is available for a period, the system should leave it blank or marked as missing rather than inventing a value, unless staff explicitly enter an estimate.

When staff compare permitted use to actual use, are there any cases where a supporting boundary layer, like a county, basin, or service area boundary, should override or change how the analysis is grouped or interpreted?

Yes, in some cases the boundary layer absolutely matters because it changes the reporting context. For example, if staff are looking at compliance or regional trends, they may need to group by basin, county, or service area instead of just by permit, especially when a permit spans more than one area. I wouldn’t say it overrides the permit data itself, but it should control how the results are summarized and interpreted when that boundary is the basis for the analysis.

When you generate outputs for different audiences, what should the system show analysts versus managers and reviewers in maps, charts, tables, or reports so that analysts can investigate in detail while the others get a concise summary for compliance or resource-management decisions?

Analysts should get the full detail, including the underlying records, site or permit identifiers, assumptions, flags, and the ability to drill down in maps, charts, and tables. Managers and reviewers should see a cleaner summary with the key totals, trends, exceptions, and any compliance indicators that support a decision without all the operational noise. If they need more detail, they can drill in, but the default view should stay concise and decision-focused.

When a conversion leaves records unresolved or changes key details like permit IDs or site names, what should staff be able to see in the review output about those changes, such as the original value, the converted value, the reason it was flagged, and any records that were quarantined?

They should be able to see the original value, the converted value, and the reason it was flagged right in the review output. If a record was quarantined because the system couldn’t resolve it confidently, that should be clearly labeled too, along with enough context for staff to decide whether to fix it manually or leave it out of the analysis. We’d want that traceability so people can trust what changed and why.

During the cutover, are there any cases where an in-flight analysis or report should stop and restart on the new version instead of finishing on the version it began with, such as if the underlying data or rules change mid-run?

Yes, if the underlying data or business rules change in a way that would make the result inconsistent, I’d expect the run to stop and restart on the new version rather than finish on the old one. That’s especially important for anything compliance-related or anything that combines multiple datasets, because we don’t want a mixed result. For routine work, though, if the run is already well underway and the version change doesn’t affect it, finishing on the original version is probably fine.
When people are working with GIS analysis and reports, what navigation, filtering, or search behavior should the system support to help them quickly find the right map area, records, or results?

It should let users search by permit number, site name, owner name, and probably county or basin, since that’s how people usually start. They should also be able to pan, zoom, and filter the map and tables together so they can narrow to the right area or subset without jumping between screens. For reports, it would help if they can save common filters or recent searches, because staff often repeat the same kinds of queries.

When someone searches the map or table, should the search match only exact values for permit, site, owner, county, and basin, or should it also support partial matches, synonyms, and any rules for handling multiple results, no matches, or saved filter sets?

It should definitely support partial matches, because staff don’t always know the exact spelling or full identifier. Exact match should still be available when they want it, but by default I’d expect flexible search on permit, site, owner, county, and basin names, and probably some common aliases or abbreviations if we can support them reliably. If there are multiple matches, the system should show a short list and let the user pick the right one, and if there’s no match it should say that clearly and keep their current filters intact. Saved filter sets would be useful too for repeated analyses, but I’d treat that as a helpful feature rather than a hard requirement unless the team says otherwise.

When a flexible search returns many partial or alias matches, what rule should decide which results are shown first, and are there any terms that should never be matched loosely because they could create confusion or risk?

The best rule would be to rank exact matches first, then close partial matches, then aliases or broader matches, so the most likely result is at the top. For the terms that should not be matched loosely, I’d be careful with permit IDs and any compliance-related identifiers, because a sloppy match there could point someone to the wrong record. Owner names and place names can be a little more forgiving, but critical IDs should stay strict unless the user explicitly widens the search.

When a user searches by a permit ID or other compliance-related identifier, what should the system do if the input is incomplete, misspelled, or formatted differently—should it return no match unless there is an exact match, or are there any controlled ways to expand that search?

For permit IDs and other compliance-related identifiers, I’d lean toward exact match by default so we don’t accidentally pull the wrong record. If we allow any expansion, it should be very controlled, like normalizing formatting differences such as spaces, dashes, or leading zeros, but not broad fuzzy matching. If the system can’t confirm an exact or normalized match, it should show no match and prompt the user to check the identifier.

What external customer tasks should the system support beyond using the GIS-based Water Use Tracking System, such as viewing or submitting information, and what should they be able to do with those tasks?

External customers should at least be able to view their own permitted water-use information and related site details, since that’s a common need. If we include submissions, they should be able to upload or enter actual use data, update contact or site information where allowed, and see the status of what they submitted. I’d expect their access to be limited to their own records, not district-wide data.

When external customers view their permitted water-use records, what specific fields or related site attributes should be visible to them, and are there any record types or details that must be hidden or redacted?

They should be able to see the basic permit information, the site location, the water use category, and the permitted quantities or limits tied to that permit. Related site attributes like county, basin, and maybe the general facility or withdrawal location would also be appropriate if they belong to that permit. I’d expect internal review notes, enforcement details, and anything about other customers’ records to be hidden, and if there are sensitive map layers or precise system details that could create security concerns, those should be redacted too.

What rules should govern which permitted water-use fields are shown to external customers versus hidden or redacted, especially when a permit includes overlapping site details, security-sensitive map information, or references that could be misinterpreted outside the regulatory context?

The rule should be that external customers only see information that is directly tied to their own permit and needed to understand their obligations. If a field could reveal internal review comments, system security details, exact sensitive infrastructure locations, or information about other permits, it should be hidden or generalized. For overlapping site details, I’d show the permit-relevant version only, and anything that could be misread outside the regulatory context should either be labeled very clearly or excluded.

For map, chart, table, and report outputs, what level of detail should external customers be allowed to interpret from their own permit information—such as exact locations, summarized trends, or labeled aggregate views—and are there any output types or labels that should be restricted, generalized, or omitted to avoid confusion or disclosure concerns?

External customers should be able to see summarized trends and permit-specific views, and in some cases a generalized map location if that’s necessary to understand their own records. I would not give them the same level of granular detail that district staff use for internal analysis, especially if it shows exact sensitive locations or combined data that could expose other facilities. Labels should stay plain and regulatory, and any internal-only report types, confidential layers, or staff-oriented notes should be restricted or omitted.

When external customers see permit information, are there any staff-only terms, labels, abbreviations, or report names that should be translated into customer-friendly wording, or should the customer-facing terminology remain exactly as it appears in the regulatory record?

Customer-facing terminology should be translated into plain language whenever the internal term might be confusing or too staff-specific. If a regulatory label is important for legal accuracy, we can keep it but add a customer-friendly explanation next to it. I would not expose internal shorthand or report names that only staff would understand unless there’s no clearer public equivalent.

When a user account needs to be created, changed, or removed, what business rules should determine who approves it, when access takes effect, and how access is handled if the person changes roles or leaves?

Access should be approved by the district for staff accounts, and for external customer accounts it should be tied to verifying that the person is authorized for that permit or company. Changes should take effect only after approval, except maybe simple contact updates, which could be immediate if they don’t affect permissions. If someone changes roles or leaves, their access should be adjusted or removed right away so they only keep the minimum access needed, and in the external case the account should follow the current authorized contact list.

When an account change is pending approval, do you want the person to keep their current access until the decision is made, or should any sensitive permissions be suspended immediately, and are there any cases where revocation must happen automatically without waiting for approval?

In most cases, they should keep their current access until the change is approved so we don’t interrupt normal work unnecessarily. But if the pending change involves reducing access because of a role change, security concern, or separation from the district, then sensitive permissions should be suspended right away. Automatic revocation should happen for clear cases like an employee leaving, a permit authorization expiring, or a customer losing authority to act for that account.
When access changes need to take effect, are there any cases where you want them to be delayed, staged, or applied at a specific time or event rather than immediately after approval?

Yes, there are a few cases where timing matters. For example, if an external customer is being granted access tied to a permit transfer or an authorized contact change, we may want it to take effect on the effective date of that change rather than right away. I’d also expect some removals or role changes to be scheduled for a specific cutoff time so we don’t disrupt a reporting cycle or ongoing review unnecessarily.
For those delayed access changes, what should happen if the effective date or cutoff time arrives while the approval or underlying permit/contact change is still pending or later gets reversed?

If the effective date arrives and the approval still isn’t complete, the change should not go live until the approval is finalized. If the underlying permit or contact change gets reversed, then any pending access change based on it should be canceled automatically. In both cases, we’d want the system to leave the current access in place or revert to the last valid state rather than partially applying anything.
